field_rule:
Field recognition may proceed with narrow paniculate habit, anthers and spikelets; to separate troublesome S. clandestinus and S. compositus use mature authenticated material, actual lemma/prickle characters and fresh-grain observations when necessary. Never identify a different taxon using a single common name 'rough dropseed'.

Field ID Lab: at the inner blade–sheath junction, hidden dropseed has a very short hair-fringed ligule with a minute membrane beneath the cilia. Choosing either the visible hair fringe or its papery base should keep it in the results; nearby collar hairs are not the ligule.

Rootstock hold: Hagenbuch & Lemke report no rhizomes for hidden dropseed in the Hill Country, whereas Flora of North America notes that rhizomes sometimes occur. The current tuft scoring is retained; do not claim a buried rhizome without an exposed, documented Hays-region same-plant specimen.

Species-level Tridens confidence requires panicle architecture PLUS mature spikelet/glume/lemma anatomy; do not identify from pigmentation alone.

Field ID Lab: white tridens grows as a bunch but may also show short, knotty underground rhizomes at the crown. Both tuft and rhizome are valid growth-form choices; check an actual dug base before asserting rhizomes in a particular photograph.

field_rule:
Supplemental field cue (Peterson and colleagues, Taxon 65, 2016) — Check the entire open panicle from its base to its tip. The published diagnosis gives 10–30 cm long and 8–20 cm wide.

Start with real source-verified Triplasiella panicles in panels 0–1, fresh Texas flowering heads in panel 5, mature reddish spikelets in panel 6 and pale fresh branching spikelets in panel 11. Panels 8–9 show the plant among other low vegetation, but the underground rootstock is obscured and neighbors may be different grasses. The stiff bristly head BEHIND panel 1 belongs to another grass; its warning arrow must remain. Open branches are a first clue, not a confirmed ID. On an attached mature flowering specimen, inspect both palea keels for smooth-to-roughened rather than densely ciliate margins, and compare the lemma midnerve tip with similar Tridens and Triplasis. Check the upper leaf sheaths for hidden spikelets, but an unopened sheath or an unphotographed structure cannot establish their absence. Do not infer the rootstock from panels 8–9 or use the separate bristly grass behind panel 1 as evidence for Triplasiella.

Females bear slender ~9–35 mm awns; males lack those long awns. Do not touch, enter habitat, or collect protected plants.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Giant cutgrass also has both sexes in its panicle but male and female are borne along the SAME branch, with the females nearer the tips.

diagnostic_checks.compare: Giant cutgrass usually has stout reedlike culms and leaves emergent ABOVE shallow swamp water, and a far larger airy head.

diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA/Kew and TPWD; floral anatomy for training from legally sourced existing verified images, not collecting protected plants

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow ONE branch to see both floral sexes
diagnostic_checks.check: Giant cutgrass is MONOECIOUS, with male and female single-flowered spikelets on the SAME main panicle BRANCHES; Kew describes male below female on each such mixed-sex branch. The open panicle is very large, ~30–60 cm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas wild-rice separates sexes on different branches of the head: lower dangling male branches and higher upright female branches.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase and TPWD both document same-branch sex arrangement; branch-sex photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure a blunt female floret and its very SHORT awn
diagnostic_checks.check: The glumes are both ABSENT/obscure. Male and female spikelets each carry one floret, around 6–8 mm in GrassBase; female lemma typically 7-veined with one SHORT (~2–3 mm) awn, male lemma awnless with anthers. Only the complete fertile floret confirms flower sex.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas wild-rice female units carry 9–35 mm awns while male branches hang below; both species can have large panicles and glumeless spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew species source checked; same-flower scale and sex detail currently needs fine diagnostic photos

diagnostic_checks.look: Check emergent rhizomatous canes, sawn blade edges and big ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Giant cutgrass is an erect, perennial 2–3 m wetland cane from elongated rhizomes. Leaf margins are minutely SAW-TOOTHED (serrulate), and the true inner ligule is a large ECILIATE 6–20 mm MEMBRANE, much longer than Phragmites' tiny ciliate membrane.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas wild-rice has long current-streaming mostly submerged leaves and is restricted to the upper San Marcos; do not use broad wetland occurrence as endemic species evidence.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew/GrassBase and TPWD contrast; connected rhizome, blade edge and 6–20 mm ligule actual photo pending
